title: Rules or Examples?
objective: After this level you can decide whether a task is better solved by writing rules or by learning from examples, and say why.
summary: Arthur Samuel's checkers program learned from its games. Rules work when you can state them exactly; examples win when the patterns are too many to write down.

cards.headline: The checkers program that learned to play better than its author
cards.body: At IBM, Arthur Samuel wrote a checkers program that recorded each position it saw and whether it led to a win or a loss, then used those records in later games. It got better the more it played. Samuel called this machine learning, a term he coined, and in 1959 he reported that a computer could learn to play better checkers than the person who wrote the program.

cards.headline: Two ways to get a job done
cards.body: The classic way is rules. A person writes every step, often as yes-or-no tests like Level 6's gates: water the garden if the soil is dry AND it is NOT raining. Machine learning flips this around. You train software, called a model, on examples, and its logic is learned from the data instead of written as explicit rules. Rules come out of a programmer's head; a model's patterns come out of its examples.

cards.headline: When rules run out
cards.body: Rules work when you can say exactly what matters. Now try writing rules for reading a stranger's handwriting: every loop, slant and smudge. IBM puts the problem plainly: as tasks get more complex, rule-based systems become brittle, because it's often impossible to write down every pattern and variable that matters. That's where learning from examples earns its keep.

cards.headline: When rules win
cards.body: Examples come at a price. Machine learning requires data, and a model needs looking after for as long as it runs. So Google's own machine learning guides advise not being afraid to launch without it: check for a non-ML solution first, because that becomes the benchmark any model has to beat. If you can state the rule exactly, like a sales tax rate, write the rule.

cards.headline: Rules or examples: sorted
learned: Samuel's checkers program learned from its own games
Rules are written; a model's patterns are learned from examples
Rules become brittle when there are too many patterns
Machine learning needs data, so try simple rules first

questions.prompt: Match each name from the rules-or-examples story with its description.

pairs.right: Check for a non-ML solution first

questions.explanation: Arthur Samuel wrote a checkers program that learned, rule-based systems become brittle as tasks get complex, and Google's own machine learning guides say to check for a non-ML solution first.

questions.prompt: A post office wants software to read messy handwritten addresses, and it has millions of labeled samples. Which approach fits, and why?

options.label: Rules, because handwriting always follows the same fixed letter shapes
options.rationale: Loops, slants and smudges vary far too much to list.

options.label: Rules, because machine learning needs no data
options.rationale: Machine learning requires data, and here the data exists.

options.label: Examples, because the patterns are too many to write down as rules
Examples, because a trained model never needs looking after
options.rationale: A model needs maintenance for as long as it runs.

questions.explanation: Handwriting has more patterns than anyone could list, which makes rules brittle, and the labeled samples give a model the data it needs.

questions.prompt: In the garden-watering rule, which logic gate makes sure both conditions hold before the sprinkler runs?

options.label: OR
options.rationale: OR would water if either condition held.

options.label: NOT
options.rationale: NOT flips a single input; it can't require two things.

options.label: A trained model
options.rationale: The watering rule is written by hand, not learned.

questions.explanation: An AND gate outputs 1 only when every input is 1, so the soil must be dry and the rain must be off.
